P:
Daṇḍaka，[Demin．of daṇḍa] 1．a （small） stick，a twig； a staff，a rod； a handle D.I，7 （a walking stick carried for ornament：see DA.I，89）； J.I，120 （sukkha° a dry twig）； II，103； III，26； DhA.III，171； Vism.353．-- aḍḍha° a （birch） rod，used as a means of beating （tāḷeti） A.I，47； II，122=M.I，87=Nd2 604=Miln.197； ubhato° two handled （of a saw） M.I，129=189； ratha° the flag-staff of a chariot Miln.27； veṇu° a jungle rope J.III，204．-- See also kudaṇḍaka a twig used for tying J.III，204．-- 2．the crossbar or bridge of a lute J.II，252，253.

--dīpikā a torch J.I，31； --madhu “honey in a branch，” a beehive DhA.I，59．（Page 312）

daṇḍakārañña.p: [Daṇḍaka+arañña] (na) Google Translate A forest named Dandaka. It is located at the confluence of the Gordavari River and the Vishnu Forest. It divides Dakkhinapatha and Mizzima. It is part of the forest between the banks of the Krigana River from Bandali Khand. Dp. The forest guarded by the king of Dankaka; Sein Ta Mani.
pn:
Daṇḍakārañña. The forest which overgrew Kaliṅga when it was laid waste through the wickedness of King Daṇḍakī (q.v.) (MN.i.378; Mil.130).

It was on the banks of the Godhāvarī and, with the Viñjhāṭavi, separated the Majjhimadesa from the Dakkhiṇāpatha. It probably comprised all the forests from Bundelkhand to the river Krishna.
a: ဒဏ္ဍက အမည်ရှိသောတော။ ယင်းသည် ဂေါဒါဝရီမြစ်ကမ်းနှင့် ဝိဉ္ဈာတောအုပ်တို့၏ အစပ်တွင် တည်ရှိ၏။ ဒက္ခိဏာပထနှင့် မဇ္ဈိမဒေသကို ပိုင်းခြားထားသည်။ ဘန်ဒေလိခန်ဒမှ ကရိဂနာမြစ်၏အကြား တောအုပ်အတွင်း အပါအဝင်ဖြစ်၏၊d.p.။ ဒဏ္ဍကမင်း စောင့်ရှောက်စိုးပိုင်သော တောအုပ်၊ စိန္တာမဏိ။

daṇḍakī.p: [Daṇḍa+ka+ī] (ti) Google Translate (A) A king who adheres to discipline. King named Dandaki. (B) Forest named Dandaki. Legendary - Look.
pn:
Daṇḍakī. King of Kumbhavatī in Kaliṅga (MN.i.378; MN-a.ii.599ff; Ja.iii.463; v.133ff; 267; Mvu.iii.363ff).

Kisavaccha, pupil of Sarabhaṅga, desiring solitude, lived in the royal park near the city, and was ill-treated by Daṇḍakī and his army while on their way to quell a rebellion, they being under the impression that insult inflicted on Kisavaccha would bring them luck.

As a result the gods were greatly incensed and destroyed the king and his country, only three people escaping death: Kisavaccha, the commander-in-chief, who was a pious follower of Kisavaccha, and a man named Rāma, who had come from Benares to Kumbhavatī. The last named was saved from destruction owing to his care for his parents. The forest which grew on the desolate land came to be called Daṇḍakārañña.
